concepts.name: Expected versus actual result
concepts.summary: Describe a test as running code with a given input and comparing the actual output to an expected output.

concepts.name: Test case anatomy
concepts.summary: Identify the setup, action and assertion parts of a simple test and what each does.

concepts.name: Pass, fail and error
concepts.summary: Recall the difference between a test passing, failing an assertion, and erroring due to an unexpected exception.

concepts.name: Bugs, defects and failures
concepts.summary: Recall the terms for a mistake in code, the faulty state it causes, and the visible failure.

concepts.name: Purpose of testing
concepts.summary: Explain that testing gathers evidence about whether software meets expectations and finds defects, but cannot prove the absence of bugs.

concepts.name: Manual versus automated testing
concepts.summary: Distinguish manual checks from automated tests and explain why automated tests are repeatable and fast to rerun.

concepts.name: Test levels overview
concepts.summary: Name unit, integration and end-to-end tests and describe in one line what scope each one covers.

misconceptions.text: If all tests pass, the software has no bugs.
Testing is only something done by a separate QA person after the code is finished.
A test that fails always means the code under test is wrong.

concepts.name: Writing unit tests with a framework
concepts.summary: Write and run unit tests using a testing framework, with assertions, test discovery and readable failure messages.

concepts.name: Test fixtures and setup
concepts.summary: Use setup and teardown to create a known starting state and clean up after each test.

concepts.name: Boundary and edge cases
concepts.summary: Choose inputs at limits such as empty, zero, maximum and off-by-one values to expose common defects.

concepts.name: Testing error handling
concepts.summary: Write tests asserting that invalid input or failing operations raise the expected errors.

concepts.name: Test independence and determinism
concepts.summary: Explain why each test should run alone, in any order, and give the same result every time.

concepts.name: Descriptive test naming
concepts.summary: Name tests so a failure report states the scenario and the expected behaviour.

concepts.name: Basic test-driven development cycle
concepts.summary: Apply the red-green-refactor loop to implement a small function by writing a failing test first.

misconceptions.text: Tests can safely share and modify global state as long as they all pass when run together.
Testing a few typical inputs is enough to show a function works.
In TDD you write all the tests for the whole program before writing any code.

concepts.name: Test doubles taxonomy
concepts.summary: Choose among dummies, stubs, fakes, spies and mocks according to what a test needs to control or observe.

concepts.name: Isolating dependencies by injection
concepts.summary: Analyse code for hard-wired dependencies and restructure it with injection so collaborators can be substituted in tests.

concepts.name: Integration test design
concepts.summary: Design tests that exercise real interactions between modules, databases or services and decide which parts to keep real.

concepts.name: Equivalence partitioning and boundaries
concepts.summary: Divide an input space into classes that behave alike and pick representative and boundary values from each.

concepts.name: Code coverage metrics
concepts.summary: Interpret statement, branch and condition coverage and analyse what a coverage figure does and does not reveal.

concepts.name: Behaviour versus implementation testing
concepts.summary: Distinguish tests that assert observable behaviour from tests coupled to internals and explain why the latter break on refactoring.

concepts.name: Diagnosing flaky tests
concepts.summary: Identify causes of flakiness such as timing, shared state, ordering and randomness and isolate them.

concepts.name: Continuous integration test runs
concepts.summary: Run the automated suite on every change in a CI pipeline and act on failures promptly.

misconceptions.text: 100% code coverage means the code is fully tested and correct.
Every dependency should be mocked in every test.
A flaky test can just be rerun until it passes, since it is not a real problem.

concepts.name: Test pyramid trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate the balance of unit, integration and end-to-end tests for a system by cost, speed, confidence and fragility.

concepts.name: End-to-end test strategy
concepts.summary: Judge which user journeys deserve end-to-end tests and design them to be stable, using controlled data and waits on conditions.

concepts.name: Contract testing
concepts.summary: Analyse how contract tests verify agreements between services without full integrated environments.

concepts.name: Property-based testing
concepts.summary: Express invariants of code as properties checked against many generated inputs, and interpret shrunk counterexamples.

concepts.name: Mutation testing
concepts.summary: Evaluate test suite strength by whether it detects injected faults, and compare this with coverage.

concepts.name: Risk-based test prioritisation
concepts.summary: Decide where to focus testing effort by weighing failure impact, likelihood and change frequency.

concepts.name: Testing legacy code
concepts.summary: Add characterization tests and create seams so untested code can be changed safely.

concepts.name: Test data management
concepts.summary: Analyse approaches to building, seeding and isolating test data so tests stay readable and independent.

misconceptions.text: The more end-to-end tests a suite has, the better, because they are the most realistic.
A high mutation score or coverage figure should be maximised everywhere as the goal of testing.

concepts.name: Designing a test strategy
concepts.summary: Create a coherent strategy across teams that sets test levels, ownership, quality gates and feedback speed for an architecture.

concepts.name: Architecting for testability
concepts.summary: Design system structure, such as ports and adapters and observability hooks, so behaviour can be verified cheaply.

concepts.name: Evaluating test suite economics
concepts.summary: Assess the cost of writing, running and maintaining tests against the defects they prevent, and retire low-value tests.

concepts.name: Testing distributed and concurrent systems
concepts.summary: Evaluate techniques such as deterministic scheduling, fault injection and simulation for finding races and partial-failure bugs.

concepts.name: Testing in production
concepts.summary: Judge when monitoring, canaries and staged rollouts complement pre-release tests and what risks they carry.

concepts.name: Building test infrastructure
concepts.summary: Create fast, parallel, hermetic test infrastructure and custom harnesses, including flaky test quarantine and selection of affected tests.

concepts.name: Testing non-functional qualities
concepts.summary: Evaluate approaches for verifying performance, reliability and security properties and their limits as evidence.

misconceptions.text: Good testing before release removes the need for monitoring and production verification.
Testability is something that can be added afterwards by writing more tests, not through design.
A single organisation-wide test ratio or coverage target suits every system.
